Johann Buchner isolates pure yellow salicin crystals
Felix Hoffmann synthesizes stable acetylsalicylic acid (Aspirin)
John Vane discovers how aspirin inhibits prostaglandins, winning Nobel Prize

sourceNote: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, Vol. 53 (1763) and Bayer Corporate Historical Archives.

title: The Island Where Evolution Kept Time
dek: On a volcanic speck in the Galápagos, Peter and Rosemary Grant spent forty consecutive summers measuring the beaks of identical finches to watch natural selection happen in real time.
heroAlt: Dramatic volcanic cliffs of Daphne Major rising from turquoise Pacific surf
heroCaption: The volcanic crater islet of Daphne Major in the Galápagos archipelago.
excerpt: Charles Darwin believed that natural selection was far too slow to ever be witnessed during a human lifetime; he thought it required hundreds of thousands of years. On Daphne Major—a desolate volcanic cinder cone forty miles off Ecuador with no fresh water and no trees—two Princeton biologists proved Darwin was wrong.

sections.heading: The Forty Summers on the Rock
sections.body: Beginning in 1973, Peter and Rosemary Grant camped on Daphne Major for six months every year. They caught, banded, measured, and weighed every single medium ground finch (Geospiza fortis) on the entire island, knowing every bird's pedigree, parentage, and precise beak depth down to the tenth of a millimeter.
sections.quote: Evolution is not something that happened only in the distant geological past; it is happening all around us, every generation, with every drought and flood.

sections.heading: The Great Drought of 1977
sections.body:
In 1977, the rains failed completely. Daphne Major received only 24 millimeters of precipitation instead of the normal 130. Small soft seeds were quickly consumed, leaving only the hard, woody fruits of the puncture vine (Tribulus cistoides).

Eighty-five percent of the finches starved to death. But birds with beaks just half a millimeter deeper than average were able to crack the armor-plated Tribulus seeds. When the surviving finches bred the following year, their offspring had beaks that were measurably, significantly larger. Natural selection had reshaped the morphology of an entire population in eighteen months.
sections.imageCaption: The precise dial calipers used by the Grants to measure finch bill depth.

sections.heading: The Fluidity of Species
sections.body: Six years later in 1983, an unprecedented El Niño brought fifty times more rain than normal, blanketing the island in vines and tiny soft seeds. Over the next decade, the Grants watched the evolutionary pendulum swing back: birds with smaller, nimble beaks out-survived the large-beaked birds. Species were not static museum specimens; they were dynamic, oscillating processes.

timeline.event: Peter and Rosemary Grant begin long-term study on Daphne Major
Major drought drives rapid evolutionary shift in beak morphology
El Niño deluge reverses selective pressures
Publication of 40 Years of Evolution: Darwin's Finches on Daphne Major

sourceNote: Princeton University Press Monographs in Population Biology and Galápagos National Park Service Records.

title: The Secret Life of Scientific Fraud
dek: From stained Piltdown jawbones to fabricated microchips, why brilliant minds risk everything to paint the data when nature refuses to cooperate.
heroAlt: Historical skull cast stained with potassium bichromate in velvet archival drawer
heroCaption: The stained cranium and orangutan jaw fragments of the Piltdown Man forgery, exposed in 1953.
excerpt: Science prides itself on being the only human endeavor with built-in self-correction. But what happens when ambition, national pride, and the desperate desire to confirm a beloved hypothesis overwhelm the stubborn honesty of the laboratory notebook?

sections.heading: The Missing Link in the Gravel Pit
sections.body:
In 1912, amateur archaeologist Charles Dawson produced skull fragments from a gravel pit in Sussex, England. British anatomical authorities hailed 'Piltdown Man' as the missing evolutionary link between ape and human—complete with a modern human braincase and a primitive ape-like jaw.

For forty years, British museums displayed the fossil with nationalistic pride. In 1953, chemical fluorine dating and microscopic analysis revealed the truth: Dawson had filed down the molars of a 500-year-old female orangutan jaw, stained it with potassium bichromate to look ancient, and planted it alongside a medieval human skull.
sections.quote: We are easily deceived by that which flatters our preexisting desires.
sections.quoteAuthor: Sir Arthur Keith (1953, upon learning of the Piltdown deception)

sections.heading: The Painter of the Guinea Pig
sections.body:
In 1974 at the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center in New York, immunologist William Summerlin claimed he had successfully transplanted skin patches between unrelated white and black mice without immune rejection. When his skeptical lab technician washed the mice, the black skin patches ran down the drain: Summerlin had drawn them on with a black felt-tip marker.

In 2001, physicist Jan Hendrik Schön at Bell Labs published dozens of papers in *Science* and *Nature* claiming breakthroughs in organic molecular semiconductors—until a reader noticed that the noise graphs in two completely different experiments were pixel-for-pixel identical.
sections.imageCaption: The identical noise waveforms in Schön's retracted Bell Labs superconductivity papers.

sections.heading: The Fragile Republic of Trust
sections.body: Scientific fraud is rarely born of simple greed; it is born of hubris—the fatal conviction that one already knows the truth and that the messy, uncooperative physical world just needs a small nudge to conform to the theory. Science survives not because scientists are saints, but because reality eventually refuses to remain forged.

timeline.event: Piltdown Man presented to the Geological Society of London
British Museum scientists expose Piltdown forgery
Summerlin mouse skin-patch fabrication exposed at Sloan-Kettering
Bell Labs inquiry panel retracts 17 papers by Jan Hendrik Schön

sourceNote: Natural History Museum London Historical Archives and Bell Labs Investigation Committee Report (2002).
